description: We are a team combining psychology, design and software to protect the minds of astronauts on long missions. Our project, Psychonaut, helps crews notice their own psychological drift early and act on it, with no link to Earth required.
summary: Psychonaut is a daily psychological health companion for astronauts on long missions, where no psychologist is on board and contact with Earth is delayed. We built a cross-platform app that detects sub-clinical drift: small changes in mood, stress, sleep, focus and motivation, measured against each crew member's own baseline. A short personality profile, a 60-second daily check-in, a reaction test and sleep data feed a risk engine that shows one of four levels, from on course to alert. Every reading explains how it is measured, why it matters and what to do, and links to the NASA risk behind it. The profile changes how the app responds, so two astronauts with the same data get different guidance. This matters because NASA rates behavioral health as a risk requiring mitigation for Mars missions, and current support depends on live contact with Earth.
details:
How it works

Before launch, each crew member gets a personality profile, either from the 20-item Mini-IPIP questionnaire in the app or from the 120-item IPIP-NEO-120 imported as a JSON file, which adds four facet scores. Three more questions set locus of control (after Rotter), preferred tone and preferred actions. Their personality profile changes how the app behaves: how soon a change is flagged, how advice is framed (data and options, or one clear step), and which actions are offered first.

Every day, the crew member logs a check-in in the Captain's log. It has six sliders: mood, stress, workload, engagement, focus and crew connection. An optional, private "Something happened at home" note can be added. A streak counts entries made, never how good the scores are. Every four days, a 3-minute reaction test measures reaction time, lapses and false starts. The design also takes in wearable data: sleep, heart rate variability, resting heart rate and activity.

The risk engine compares each indicator with the person's own baseline and gives one of four levels: on course, drifting, off course or alert. The levels combine into one "degrees off course" number. Every reading explains how it is measured, why it matters and what to do now, and links to the NASA risk it relates to. Psychonaut also flags a mismatch when someone reports feeling fine while their sleep or reaction time has been off baseline for a week. At alert level it always shows one fixed message: "Tell your crew medical officer and prepare a summary for Earth."

Trends shows 14 nights of sleep and the reaction test history against the personal baseline, with three course-correction actions to choose from. Ship morale shows the crew's wellbeing as one anonymous number and a shared weekly goal, with no leaderboard.

Psychonaut runs fully offline on a phone, a tablet or a crew console. The written daily reading comes from rules on the device. The app is also built to let a crew choose an on-board AI model that keeps everything on the vehicle, or a cloud model for use on Earth, and every AI reading is checked so that it never diagnoses or gives medication advice.

Benefits and impact

NASA rates behavioral health as a risk that requires mitigation for Mars missions, and reports that symptoms below the level of diagnosis have already affected missions. Psychonaut targets those small changes and does not depend on real-time contact with Earth. On Earth, the same approach can help people far from care, such as remote communities and older adults living alone.

What makes it creative

The personality profile is loaded per person and changes the app's thresholds and wording, so two crew members with the same data receive different guidance. A ship metaphor (captain's log, calibration, course correction) keeps crews engaged through long routine periods and rewards honest check-ins, never good scores.

Tools

Flutter 3.50 and Dart, one codebase for iOS, Android, macOS, Linux and web, with a Material 3 dark theme. Packages: flutter_riverpod for state, go_router for navigation, fl_chart for charts, shared_preferences for on-device storage, file_picker for profile import, http for optional model calls, and intl with flutter_localizations for six languages. Fonts are bundled for offline use: Inter, Space Grotesk, Noto Sans Arabic and Noto Sans JP. All 220 unit and widget tests pass, with 99.75% line coverage of the app code. The code was written with GitHub Copilot and reviewed by the team.

What we considered

Privacy: by default everything stays on the device, the data is never used to rank the crew, and the Crew screen shows one anonymous group number. The cloud model is optional and, if chosen, sends scores and the personality profile but never the name, role or private notes. Safety: the app never diagnoses, names a disorder or gives medication advice; generated text that breaks these rules is rejected, every reading shows its source, and the alert message is fixed. Science: the sleep ranges, the 500 ms lapse and the Mini-IPIP items come from published research; the baseline, drift rules, personality cut-offs and mission-phase rule are our own design assumptions and have not been validated.

Prototype status

This prototype runs on fictional sample data, and only sleep is scored from the wearable data so far. The on-board and cloud AI connections have been tested against a test server, not yet a real model. The five non-English translations are machine-drafted and await review by native speakers. Locus of control comes from one self-rated question, and the reaction test is not a validated instrument. The app has been built for macOS, web, iOS and Android and run on macOS and Chrome; it has not yet been built on Linux.

Next

Real wearable data from Apple Health and Health Connect, an on-board AI model tested on real hardware, a summary for the crew medical officer sent with the crew member's consent, and validation of the thresholds with analog mission data.
